questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe the prokaryotic cell plan
questions.stem: A clinic note describes a bacterium recovered from a wound swab and asks what the prokaryotic cell plan includes.

options.text: A cell with no nucleus, DNA in a nucleoid region, ribosomes and a membrane, and no membrane-bound organelles.
A cell with a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria and a rigid wall of cellulose.
options.misconception: describes a eukaryotic plant cell instead of a bacterium

options.text: A cell that has a nucleus but no mitochondria, since bacteria respire without organelles.
options.misconception: halves the eukaryote organelles but keeps the nucleus

options.text: A cell with a nucleus, chloroplasts and endoplasmic reticulum, typical of green plants.
options.misconception: lists plant organelles for a prokaryote

questions.explanation: Bacteria lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, keeping DNA in a nucleoid region with ribosomes and a plasma membrane. Their wall, when present, is peptidoglycan rather than cellulose.
questions.hint: Ask what the bacterial cell lacks.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret antibiotic sensitivity as evidence about the wall
questions.stem: A note reports that a culture was destroyed by penicillin while a nearby isolate grew well, and asks what this shows.

options.text: The penicillin-sensitive isolate had no cell wall at all, since penicillins only act on walls.
options.misconception: confuses a thin wall with no wall at all

options.text: The sensitive isolate likely had a thin peptidoglycan layer, which penicillin blocked from being built.
The resistant isolate had a thick capsule that absorbed the penicillin before it reached the wall.
options.misconception: credits a capsule with absorbing the antibiotic

options.text: The resistant isolate had no peptidoglycan and instead used a cellulose wall for support.
options.misconception: claims bacteria build cellulose walls

questions.explanation: Penicillin blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking, so a bacterium with a thin or exposed wall stops growing while a protected one survives. Resistance can also come from modified targets, not from the wall alone.
questions.hint: Think about what penicillin actually blocks.

questions.learningObjective: Identify ribosomes in a labelled bacterial diagram
questions.stem: A labelled diagram of a bacterium in the note marks a small dense particle in the cytoplasm, drawn much smaller than the nucleoid.

options.text: The marked particle is a mitochondrion, which supplies energy to the bacterial cell.
options.misconception: imports a eukaryotic organelle into a bacterium

options.text: The marked particle is a mesosome, a fold of the membrane used for respiration.
options.misconception: invents a membrane organelle as the marked body

options.text: The marked particle is a storage granule, a reserve of nutrients held in the cytoplasm.
options.misconception: confuses ribosomes with nutrient reserves

options.text: The marked particle is a ribosome, the bacterial site of protein assembly.

questions.explanation: The tiny dense particles in bacterial cytoplasm are 70S ribosomes, where proteins are built on messenger RNA. Bacteria lack mitochondria and other membrane-bound organelles.
questions.hint: Bacterial protein synthesis happens on small particles.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a false description of the bacterial capsule
questions.stem: A note is returned because it says the bacterial capsule is a structure that pumps ions out of the cell.

options.text: The note is fine, because capsules are membrane pumps that export antibiotics and waste.
options.misconception: describes the capsule as an active ion pump

options.text: The note should say the capsule builds peptidoglycan for the cell wall during growth.
options.misconception: assigns wall synthesis to the capsule

options.text: The note is wrong, because the capsule is a protective outer layer that aids attachment and resists phagocytosis.
The note should say the capsule stores the bacterial DNA as a separate ring.
options.misconception: confuses the capsule with a plasmid

questions.explanation: A capsule is a gelatinous protective coat outside the cell wall that helps bacteria adhere and resist immune engulfment. Ion pumping belongs to membrane proteins, and plasmid DNA sits elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask what the coat outside the wall does.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why viruses are classified as acellular
questions.stem: One paragraph in the note asks the team to explain in writing why a virus is described as acellular.

answer.exemplar: A virus has no cellular machinery of its own. Its particle consists of a nucleic acid genome wrapped in protein subunits, sometimes inside a lipid envelope, and it cannot make proteins or generate energy on its own. It can only reproduce inside a host cell that supplies the machinery, which is why viruses are classified as acellular rather than as very small cells.

questions.explanation: Viruses carry a genome and protein coat but no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolism, so they cannot grow or divide on their own. Reproduction requires a host cell, so they lie outside the cellular world.
questions.hint: Ask what the particle lacks compared with a cell.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the different Gram reactions
questions.stem: A clinic note asks why one isolate stains purple and another stains pink in the same Gram stain run.

options.text: The purple one is Gram negative because the counterstain took over, while the pink one is Gram positive.
options.misconception: reverses the Gram reaction of the two isolates

options.text: The purple one is a larger cell, and the pink one is a smaller cell of the same species.
options.misconception: believes cell size alone sets the stain colour

options.text: The purple one keeps the crystal violet complex in a thick peptidoglycan layer, while the pink one loses it.
The purple one has a capsule, and the pink one has a naked cell wall with no peptidoglycan.
options.misconception: ties capsule presence to the purple reaction

questions.explanation: Gram positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan layer that holds the crystal violet complex after alcohol decolourisation, so they stay purple. Gram negative cells have a thin layer and take up the counterstain.
questions.hint: Think about how much peptidoglycan each type keeps.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Name the main bacterial cell shapes
questions.stem: A microscopy note describes three isolates: one rod shaped, one spherical and one spiral with rigid cell walls.

options.text: The note shows the isolates differ only in size, since all bacterial cells are spherical by nature.
options.misconception: claims all bacterial cells share one shape

options.text: The note shows three distinct morphologies, called bacillus, coccus and spirillum, that aid identification.
The note shows the isolates are different species, since a species is defined by cell shape alone.
options.misconception: defines a species by cell shape alone

options.text: The note shows the spiral organism is a eukaryote, because only eukaryotes can be spiral.
options.misconception: treats a spiral shape as proof of a eukaryote

questions.explanation: Bacteria come in characteristic shapes that help identification: bacilli are rods, cocci are spheres and spirilla are spirals. Shape is a clue, never a definition of a species.
questions.hint: Name the three shape categories.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an endospore in a labelled diagram
questions.stem: A diagram in the note shows a rod shaped bacterium with a small dense oval inside, drawn with the outer cell outline contracted around it.

options.text: The diagram shows an endospore, a dormant resistant structure that can survive harsh conditions.
The diagram shows a plasmid, a small ring of DNA that carries accessory genes.
options.misconception: mistakes the dense body for a ring of plasmid DNA

options.text: The diagram shows a capsule, a swollen polysaccharide coat surrounding the cell.
options.misconception: confuses the contracted outline with a capsule

options.text: The diagram shows a dividing cell, with the oval being the new daughter cell.
options.misconception: reads the dormant structure as a division stage

questions.explanation: An endospore appears as a dense oval inside the cell and is released when the parent breaks down. It survives heat and drying, while plasmids are rings of DNA and capsules are surface coats.
questions.hint: The structure survives heat and drying.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct the function given for bacterial flagella
questions.stem: A note is challenged because it claims that bacterial flagella are used mainly to exchange genetic material.

options.text: The note is fine, because flagella fuse with neighbouring cells to move DNA across.
options.misconception: confuses flagellar rotation with conjugation

options.text: The note should say flagella carry the chromosome around inside the cell.
options.misconception: claims flagella carry the bacterial chromosome

options.text: The note should say flagella digest the peptidoglycan wall as the cell grows.
options.misconception: invents a digestive role for flagella

options.text: The note is wrong, because flagella drive motility, while pili handle attachment and the transfer of DNA between cells.

questions.explanation: Flagella are rotary motors that drive swimming and swarming through the liquid. Pili or fimbriae attach the cell to surfaces and to other cells, and a sex pilus helps move DNA during conjugation.
questions.hint: Match each appendage to its usual job.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a bacterial cell differs from a eukaryotic one
questions.stem: The teaching file asks the team to write out what separates a bacterial cell from a plant or animal cell.

answer.exemplar: Bacteria have no membrane-bound nucleus, so their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid region, and they also lack mitochondria, chloroplasts and endoplasmic reticulum. Their genetic material is a single circular chromosome, their ribosomes are smaller than those of eukaryotes, and they divide by binary fission rather than mitosis.

questions.explanation: The defining difference is the absence of a membrane-bound nucleus and other organelles, plus a circular chromosome, smaller ribosomes and division by binary fission.
questions.hint: Focus on what the bacterial cell does not contain.

questions.learningObjective: Count the amino acids in a peptidoglycan side chain
questions.stem: One calculation in the note asks how many amino acids form the tetrapeptide side chain attached to each sugar unit of peptidoglycan.
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan repeats a disaccharide backbone of two sugars, each carrying a short chain of four amino acids. These chains are cross-linked by transpeptidase, the step that beta-lactam antibiotics block.
questions.hint: The name tetrapeptide gives the number away.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the selective toxicity of ribosome-targeting antibiotics
questions.stem: A note asks why a bacterium responds to some antibiotics that have no effect on the patient's own cells.

options.text: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S with a different protein and rRNA structure than human 80S ribosomes.
Bacterial ribosomes are larger than human ribosomes, so they take up more of the antibiotic.
options.misconception: claims bacterial ribosomes are larger than eukaryotic ones

options.text: Bacterial ribosomes are made of DNA, so the antibiotic binds to the genetic material directly.
options.misconception: says ribosomes are made of DNA rather than RNA and protein

options.text: Bacterial ribosomes lack rRNA, so the antibiotic blocks the cell wall instead.
options.misconception: describes ribosomes as DNA structures that build walls

questions.explanation: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, with 50S and 30S subunits, while human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S. That difference lets some antibiotics block bacterial protein synthesis selectively.
questions.hint: Compare the bacterial and human ribosome sizes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain mucoid colonies and phagocyte resistance
questions.stem: A note describes an isolate that forms a turbid, gelatinous layer around colonies on agar and is resistant to phagocytosis.

options.text: The turbidity comes from a thick peptidoglycan wall, which makes the colony viscous.
options.misconception: attributes the gel to the peptidoglycan layer

options.text: The turbidity comes from a polysaccharide capsule, which protects the bacterium from immune engulfment.
The turbidity comes from bacterial spores released into the agar as the colony grows.
options.misconception: confuses capsule material with spores in the agar

options.text: The turbidity comes from many free plasmid molecules released by the dividing cells.
options.misconception: explains colony turbidity with free plasmid DNA

questions.hint: Look for a mucoid colony with immune resistance.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an enveloped virus particle in a diagram
questions.stem: A labelled diagram in the note shows a small sphere with a protein coat of repeating subunits, a coiled strand inside and a lipid bilayer surrounding both.

options.text: The diagram shows a bacterium, with the coil representing its nucleoid chromosome.
options.misconception: reads the particle as a bacterium rather than a virus

options.text: The diagram shows a flagellum, with the coat forming the helix of the filament.
options.misconception: confuses the capsid with a flagellar filament

options.text: The diagram shows a spore, with the bilayer forming the tough outer spore coat.
options.misconception: mistakes the lipid envelope for a spore coat

options.text: The diagram shows an enveloped virus particle, with capsid, genome and lipid envelope.

questions.explanation: Protein subunits forming a coat around a nucleic acid strand with a lipid bilayer outside describe an enveloped virus particle. Bacteria are much larger and have walls, and flagella are filaments.
questions.hint: Look for capsid subunits and an envelope.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a false description of plasmids
questions.stem: A note is rejected because it says a plasmid is the main chromosome of a bacterium and is always essential.

options.text: The note is fine, because plasmids carry the genes needed for survival in every habitat.
options.misconception: describes plasmids as universally essential genetic material

options.text: The note should say plasmids are always present and are needed to build the cell wall.
options.misconception: claims every bacterium requires its plasmids to grow

options.text: The note is wrong, because plasmids are separate small circles of DNA that are usually dispensable.
The note should say plasmids replace the bacterial chromosome after a mutation occurs.
options.misconception: treats plasmids as replacements for the bacterial chromosome

questions.explanation: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules that replicate alongside the chromosome and often carry accessory genes such as antibiotic resistance. Most can be lost without harm.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if the plasmid is removed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe the steps of the Gram stain
questions.stem: A protocol asks the team to write out the steps of the Gram stain and why each one matters.

answer.exemplar: The primary stain, crystal violet, colours every cell purple. Decolourising with alcohol or acetone dissolves the outer membrane of Gram negative cells and washes the complex out of their thin peptidoglycan, while Gram positive cells retain it because their thick peptidoglycan traps the dye. The counterstain, safranin, then paints the decolourised Gram negative cells pink while the Gram positive cells stay purple.

questions.explanation: The stain works because decolourisation removes the complex from thin-walled cells but not thick ones, so the counterstain colours only the cells that lost the purple dye.
questions.hint: Each step exploits differences in wall thickness.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a diagram of a released endospore

options.misconception: reads the spore and ghost as two daughters

options.text: The diagram shows a cell filled with a storage granule of stored nutrients.
options.misconception: confuses the released spore with a nutrient granule

options.text: The diagram shows a mature endospore released after the parent cell lysed.
The diagram shows a cell infected by a virus, with the oval as a phage particle.
options.misconception: mistakes a bacterial spore for a viral particle

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish attachment pili from the sex pilus
questions.stem: A note is challenged because it states that all pili on a bacterium are used for bacterial conjugation.

options.text: The note is fine, because pili and fimbriae are simply two names for the same transfer structure.
options.misconception: treats attachment pili and sex pili as identical

options.text: The note is wrong, because most pili or fimbriae attach the cell to surfaces, while a sex pilus transfers DNA.
The note should say conjugation is performed by flagella rather than by pili.
options.misconception: assigns conjugation to flagellar structures

options.misconception: gives pili a role in wall synthesis

questions.hint: Ask whether the pili are for sticking or for transfer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a prokaryotic cell from a labelled diagram
questions.stem: A labelled sketch in the note shows a cell with an outer capsule, a cell wall, a plasma membrane, scattered ribosomes and a large irregular region of DNA with no membrane.

options.text: The diagram shows a prokaryote, since the DNA lies in a nucleoid region with no nuclear membrane.
The diagram shows a eukaryote, since the DNA is gathered in a distinct nucleus.
options.misconception: mistakes the nucleoid for a membrane-bound nucleus

options.text: The diagram shows a fungal cell, since the thick wall is made of chitin.
options.misconception: assigns fungal chitin to a bacterial wall

options.text: The diagram shows a plant cell, since the outer coat is a cellulose wall.
options.misconception: assigns cellulose to the wall in the drawing

questions.explanation: A nucleoid region with no surrounding membrane is the hallmark of a prokaryotic cell, together with free ribosomes and no mitochondria. Such a wall is peptidoglycan, not chitin or cellulose.
questions.hint: The DNA has no membrane around it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a false description of the cell wall
questions.stem: A note says that the peptidoglycan wall of a bacterium is a flexible layer that only gives the cell its shape.

options.text: The note is fine, because bacterial walls are soft and change shape at each division.
options.misconception: describes the bacterial wall as soft and flexible

options.text: The note should say the wall is made of lipids, like the cell membrane.
options.misconception: claims bacterial walls are built from lipids

options.text: The note should say the wall is optional and only some bacteria have any structure.
options.misconception: believes bacteria have no wall at all

options.text: The note is wrong, because the rigid peptidoglycan wall resists osmotic lysis and holds the shape.

questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan is a strong cross-linked mesh that holds a bacterial cell's shape and stops water rushing in and bursting it. Since it is not membrane-like, lysozyme and beta-lactams work against it.
questions.hint: Think about what happens if the wall is removed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe bacterial protein synthesis
questions.stem: For the education file the note asks the team to write out how a bacterium makes protein on its ribosomes.

answer.exemplar: A bacterium transcribes its chromosomal DNA into messenger RNA, and that message binds to the small 30S subunit of a 70S ribosome. The large 50S subunit then joins, and the ribosome moves along the message, joining amino acids into a polypeptide in the order the codons specify. The finished protein folds and is used inside the cell or exported.

questions.explanation: Protein synthesis in bacteria follows transcription then translation on 70S ribosomes made of 30S and 50S subunits. The message dictates the amino acid order, and the finished chain folds into a working protein.
questions.hint: Start with copying the gene into a message.

questions.hint: Subtract the bare diameter from the capsulated one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how endospores support survival
questions.stem: A teaching note asks the team to write out how a bacterial endospore helps an organism survive.

answer.exemplar: An endospore is a dormant, highly resistant structure that a bacterium forms when conditions become unfavourable. It dehydrates its core, deposits calcium dipicolinate and thickens its coat, and shuts down metabolism, allowing it to survive heat, drying, radiation and chemicals for years. When conditions improve the spore germinates, and the cell resumes growth and division.

questions.explanation: The spore protects the genome in a dormant state through dehydration, thick coats and resistant chemicals, so the cell survives conditions that kill growing bacteria. It germinates when conditions improve.
questions.hint: Think about what the dormant state protects against.

questions.hint: Multiply the average per cell by the number of cells.

options.misconception: claims the lysozyme treatment removed a whole wall

options.text: The lysed isolate had exposed peptidoglycan, while the intact one was shielded by an outer membrane or capsule.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bacteria divide by binary fission
questions.stem: One teaching point in the note asks the team to write out why bacterial replication takes place by binary fission.

answer.exemplar: Bacteria divide by binary fission: the single circular chromosome is copied, the two copies are pulled apart as the cell elongates, and a cross wall of new peptidoglycan grows in the middle, splitting one cell into two genetically near-identical daughters. Because no spindle, nuclear envelope or mitosis is involved, division is quick and does not pass through a metaphase stage.

questions.explanation: Binary fission needs no spindle or nucleus: the chromosome is copied, the cell elongates, and a peptidoglycan cross wall separates the copies, producing two near-identical daughters without mitosis.
questions.hint: Think about what is absent from the dividing cell.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain selective toxicity of antibacterial drugs
questions.stem: A sidebar in the note asks the team to write out why some antibiotics kill bacteria without harming the patient.

answer.exemplar: Selective toxicity comes from differences between bacterial and human machinery. Antibiotics such as streptomycin, tetracyclines and macrolides bind specifically to the 70S bacterial ribosome and block protein synthesis, while the corresponding human 80S ribosomes are spared. questions.explanation: Selective toxicity works because bacteria and human cells differ in target structure, so agents that hit the 70S ribosome or the cell wall leave human cells largely untouched. Bacteria also lack the enzymes human cells use.
